dossier_audits.name: Eastern Han

existing_interval.label: 25–220 CE
existing_interval.note: Eastern phase of Han rule, not the beginning or end of Chinese society.

rubric.orientation: The Luoyang court and models of rural estates answer the opening question at two different scales.
rubric.explanation: Tower, well and granary connect a household’s continued provision to unnamed work. The memorial supplies a distinct mechanism for moving surplus toward the state.
rubric.evidence: Columbia’s longer translated excerpt explicitly proposes honoring grain or pardoning an offense in exchange for deliveries. The teaching introduction dates Chao Cuo’s proposal to 178 BCE.
rubric.chronology_geography: 25–220 CE encloses the Eastern Han phase. The 178 and 81 BCE texts are explicitly earlier Western Han evidence.
rubric.perspective: The memorial addresses the ruler and characterizes farmers and merchants for a political purpose. The owners who commissioned burial models are unusually visible.
rubric.reading: The models provide a concrete short entrance. The deeper discussion asks who possessed enough surplus to benefit from a proposed policy.
rubric.activity: Each of the three objects supplies a visible feature and a household need. Naming a task left unseen is possible without assigning a named worker.
rubric.connections: The Han/Xin context clarifies the interruption. Comparing Rome’s named portraits with elite Han burials keeps both sample biases visible.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: Colima architectural models

existing_interval.label: 200 BCE–200 CE
existing_interval.note: Date of the selected temple model; not a lifespan assigned to an entire people.

rubric.orientation: The stair, levels and roof invite a concrete question about a small ceramic building from western Mexico.
rubric.explanation: Making an offering and preparing a chamber explain how a model might participate in a ceremony. The suggested burner function has its own test.
rubric.evidence: The Huitzilapa researchers report six interments in two chambers. Microscopy distinguished cotton and agave while many presumed food remains permitted only broad identifications.
rubric.chronology_geography: The current accession range ends at 200 CE. The 2015 caption extends it to 300 CE. Huitzilapa in Jalisco supplies a separately dated comparison.
rubric.perspective: The differences among funerary offerings allow questions about status. Ancestor relationships are an attributed interpretation across varied communities.
rubric.reading: Following the shape and making an observation precede the optional abstract-based discussion of burial materials and competing date ranges.
rubric.activity: The two views and a three-way sorting task distinguish a visible roof, a proposed lid and an unknown tomb. The learner can offer a possible test using the explanation.
rubric.connections: Hopewell offers a comparison about deposited objects and organized work. The regional locator supplies no shared origin with that example.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: The Roman world around 200

existing_interval.label: 193–235 CE
existing_interval.note: Severan political period; this is not the full lifespan of Roman history.

rubric.orientation: Rome’s court and the earlier Egyptian portrait give the reader named people and distinct locations.
rubric.explanation: Military backing, public representation and legal status explain why a dynasty needed more than a portrait and why occupation alone cannot classify a worker.
rubric.evidence: The Met’s inscription discussion identifies Eutyches as a freedman and offers alternative readings of the following names and signature. The deeper section appropriately attributes the interpretation.
rubric.chronology_geography: 193–235 CE is the Severan frame. The Egyptian portrait’s approximately 100–150 date precedes it, and 212 citizenship is separately situated.
rubric.perspective: The provincial portrait widens the court narrative, while commemoration still gives selective access to the boy’s life.
rubric.reading: Two faces provide the short comparison. The deeper reading distinguishes legal freedom, social position and a possible manumission witness.
rubric.activity: The learner can use materials, text and pose before using the two captions to distinguish burial from imperial display.
rubric.connections: The earlier Roman frame and Han comparison share a question about resource demands while leaving the sources for each polity distinct.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: Palmyra

existing_interval.label: 2nd–3rd centuries CE
existing_interval.note: Window of the selected funerary relief, not the city’s entire history.

rubric.orientation: The family relief identifies a Syrian city through a particular commemorative commission. The civic tariff supplies a separate public setting.
rubric.explanation: Tax schedules and honors for caravan organizers give different evidence for local exchange and long-distance movement.
rubric.evidence: The Met’s numbered transliteration and English gloss separate Zabdibol’s ancestors from Mokimu, Tadmur and Alayyat. Naming children is warranted independently of pose.
rubric.chronology_geography: The object’s second–third-century range differs from the explicitly dated 137 council tariff and the events of 272–273.
rubric.perspective: The tribute of a stone memorial and public honorific inscriptions privileges families and merchants with resources. The text marks the absence of a population-wide literacy measure.
rubric.reading: The first task uses a bounded family group. The deeper Berlin relief discussion explains why a possible tutor or tablet on another object cannot identify the selected children.
rubric.activity: The supplied names answer the kinship question. A tax question can be assigned to the tariff without assuming the depicted family financed a caravan.
rubric.connections: The civic context and exchange-network place study make the distinction between a family’s memorial and a schematic regional route explicit.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: Kushan worlds

existing_interval.label: Early centuries CE
existing_interval.note: Focus window for imperial Kushan contexts; boundaries and rulers’ chronologies are debated.

rubric.orientation: The coin anchors a broad Gandhara/Kushan frame, with contrasting evidence from named Bactrian temple sites.
rubric.explanation: The Rabatak royal orders and Surkh Kotal water shortage explain how commands, construction and commemoration relate.
rubric.evidence: Sims-Williams’s published Surkh Kotal edition distinguishes the Burzmihr and Mihraman formulae across versions. The dossier distinguishes credited work from proof of who physically dug the well.
rubric.chronology_geography: The selected coin is about 130 CE. Inscription year one, a possible year six and year 31 are not interchangeable modern dates.
rubric.perspective: An official and a writer are identifiable, while the workforce and worshippers are not fully represented by this record.
rubric.reading: Both sides of a coin give the family a visible start. The deeper discussion introduces language versus script through a qualified epigraphic reading.
rubric.activity: The well capsule specifies the problem, action and official. The activity never requires readers to guess a reverse deity or undocumented findspot.
rubric.connections: The temple context and comparison can follow the communication question without transferring the Berlin coin’s deity or provenance to the Met specimen.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: Aksum and Adulis

existing_interval.label: 1st–8th centuries CE
existing_interval.note: Broad conventional flourishing in the consulted architectural essay; not exact founding and extinction.

rubric.orientation: The first-century port account names Adulis and the inland city. Beta Samati introduces an excavated town distinct from both.
rubric.explanation: Grinding stones, storage caches and workshop debris explain how production and provision supported an inland settlement.
rubric.evidence: The excavators’ Area A discussion records slag and glass wasters and interprets production alongside domestic activity. Figure 4 pairs two faces of each coin. The evidence supports local work without assigning every glass object a local origin.
rubric.chronology_geography: The early Periplus, fourth-century texts and late deposits are kept on their own timescales. The unrelated Roman bottle is identified as a type comparison.
rubric.perspective: Trade writing favors merchant concerns. The archaeological account reveals household and workshop activity but does not identify each worker.
rubric.reading: Five coins give readers a tangible sequence of manufacture, deposition and excavation. The separate monuments and scripts provide the deeper reading.
rubric.activity: The exercise asks for five objects rather than ten photographed faces and permits the circulation time to remain unknown.
rubric.connections: Red Sea context links highland and port. The evidence for ordinary production broadens a comparison that could otherwise rest entirely on royal inscriptions.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: Teotihuacan

existing_interval.label: c. 100 BCE–800 CE
existing_interval.note: Broad city chronology in Barnes’s essay; buildings and population changed within it.

rubric.orientation: The city question starts with household spaces and distinguishes the greenstone face from the excavations at Tlajinga.
rubric.explanation: Blade manufacture, access to imported materials and drains show how residents participated in the city. The floor study tests competing uses of a neighborhood platform.
rubric.evidence: The excavation project identifies variable masonry and adobe, restricted luxury goods, central courtyards and drains emptying onto the Street of the Dead in Compounds 17 and 18.
rubric.chronology_geography: The monument and apartment construction phases overlap a long urban interval. The mask and the modern composite map each receive separate dating qualifications.
rubric.perspective: The actual work of making blades is visible in byproducts. Household apprenticeship is an interpretation. The excavated sample cannot give the names or powers of decision makers.
rubric.reading: A straightforward home-and-street account prepares readers for the deeper discussion of testing a building function against different classes of evidence.
rubric.activity: The family draws a modern relationship diagram using selected features, labels an inferred maintenance arrangement and leaves one labor question open.
rubric.connections: The Chavín textile and Moche comparisons offer material evidence of productive work and social organization at different places and scales.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: Moche communities

existing_interval.label: 1st–8th centuries CE
existing_interval.note: Broad cultural flourishing; not a claim of one unchanging centralized state.

rubric.orientation: Named northern coastal river valleys establish the regional setting and distinguish stylistic similarities from political unity.
rubric.explanation: Tools, moulds, unfired pieces and firing failures distinguish pottery production at a site from merely finding finished vessels there.
rubric.evidence: Bernier’s workshop discussion distinguishes a partially excavated fineware installation from utilitarian remains visible on the surface. This supports production at Huacas de Moche while leaving the two museum vessels’ workshops unknown.
rubric.chronology_geography: Huacas de Moche production and Jequetepeque political models are attributed to separate sites within a long regional frame.
rubric.perspective: Household and food-processing evidence complements elite imagery. The dossiers attribute proposed ritual interpretations and local political coordination.
rubric.reading: Visible vessel surfaces make the short entry usable. Comparing exchange, architectural imagery and stratified workshop evidence gives a deeper investigation.
rubric.activity: The answer key separates on-site production, the tentative renewal interpretation and the unsupported inference of a common ruler.
rubric.connections: The valley/work context and paired comparison use recurring craft and material questions without positing one centre of manufacture.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: Đông Sơn drum traditions

existing_interval.label: c. 500 BCE–300 CE
existing_interval.note: Catalogue date of the miniature; wider drum traditions have their own chronologies.

rubric.orientation: The four frogs and the miniature’s height introduce a question about uses of a repeated drum form across different places.
rubric.explanation: Tools inside one drum, a drum over a wooden vessel elsewhere, and moulds discarded at a workshop show different stages in the lives of objects.
rubric.evidence: The 2024 excavation report identifies inner and outer mould fragments, crucible and furnace fragments and slag in a waste layer with third–sixth-century material.
rubric.chronology_geography: The late Luy Lâu reference extends past the miniature’s broad interval. The two published Ngọc Lũ discovery-location accounts disagree and remain distinct.
rubric.perspective: Woodworking and textile production appear alongside casting. The preserved objects cannot identify individual artisans, and no bones survived in the presumed Phú Chánh graves.
rubric.reading: A measurement and two contrasting deposits anchor the family reading. The deeper discussion distinguishes stylistic dates from dated associated material.
rubric.activity: A ruler helps a pair imagine the small object. Two separately labelled context cards prevent evidence from one burial or hoard being assigned to the miniature.
rubric.connections: Hopewell deposits and Shang bronzes support comparisons about context and interpretation. Neither supplies the Vietnamese object’s route or use.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: Benin ivory and Portuguese patrons

existing_interval.label: c. 1525–1600 CE
existing_interval.note: Catalogue date of the selected saltcellar; not the kingdom’s founding or end.

rubric.orientation: Benin City and an Edo saltcellar give the opening question a specific setting.
rubric.explanation: The supports and European dress connect carving choices to the court’s patronage and an export audience.
rubric.evidence: The museum describes specialist guilds under palace control, ceremonial uses and royal patronage. The saltcellar itself has a qualified court attribution.
rubric.chronology_geography: The catalogue range c.1525–1600, 1897 invasion and 1972 accession are three different pieces of history.
rubric.perspective: The reading leaves the unnamed maker, buyer and intermediaries open.
rubric.reading: The master-name explanation makes attribution intelligible. The provenance paragraph correctly requires evidence specific to this object.
rubric.activity: Seeing some figures and reading the total in a catalogue supplies two distinguishable evidence cards.
rubric.connections: The Benin court context explains authority behind the object. Compare how patrons and makers shaped a commission.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: Kongo: translating Christianity

existing_interval.label: From the royal baptism of 1491 CE
existing_interval.note: A documented starting episode for this investigation. No single terminal year is assigned to an evolving religious tradition.

rubric.orientation: The brass crucifix lets a reader ask who gave an adopted symbol meaning. The account begins with interpreters, students and religious practice.
rubric.explanation: Raised figures and incised lines supply an example of a maker’s choices. Afonso’s letters show how diplomacy, schooling and trafficking intersected.
rubric.evidence: In the translated supplement Afonso asks for medical workers and supplies in addition to describing kidnapping. This concrete request supports the discussion of diplomacy and care.
rubric.chronology_geography: The July and October 1526 letters have specific settings; the cross has a broad object date. The chronology avoids dating its design by progressive resemblance to European forms.
rubric.perspective: Afonso’s position helps explain his concerns about free people and his authority. The letters cannot speak for those seized.
rubric.reading: The adult sections identify the missing translator and critical edition, and give reasons to treat descriptions of religious change as interpretations.
rubric.activity: A child can distinguish the smaller cast figures from a written request for officials to inspect purchases.
rubric.connections: The return prompt connects changes in meaning with the people negotiating religious practices.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: An ocean route to Calicut

existing_interval.label: 1497–1499 CE
existing_interval.note: Dates of da Gama’s voyage in the consulted chronology; not the beginning of Indian Ocean exchange.

rubric.orientation: Asking whose route was new introduces existing port communities and the knowledge on which the expedition relied.
rubric.explanation: Supplies, the pilot’s services and multilingual conversations explain work on both sides of the ocean crossing.
rubric.evidence: Ravenstein’s translated journal describes a convict taken to two men from Tunis able to communicate in Castilian and Genoese. This supports a specific encounter at Calicut.
rubric.chronology_geography: Malindi and Calicut are distinct stops. The late-fifteenth-century voyage, later manuscript copy and 1898 edition are dated separately.
rubric.perspective: The writer’s Christian framing and account of hostage-taking complicate the reader’s understanding of help and consent.
rubric.reading: The deeper reading explains why a navigator’s visibility at one moment leaves a partial biography.
rubric.activity: A child can label one shore-based task and locate its ports without treating the schematic as a reconstructed ship track.
rubric.connections: The merchant-perspective prompt invites a different question about the arrival. The preceding text explains why local testimony would be needed to substantiate an answer.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: Silver, porcelain and the Pacific

existing_interval.label: 1565–1815 CE
existing_interval.note: Historical range of the galleon trade. The C7 display clips at 1800; that is not its end.

rubric.orientation: The Acapulco locator and silver/porcelain question introduce a multistage network.
rubric.explanation: Shipyards, provisioning and the 1595 wreck make transport depend on actual labor and vessels.
rubric.evidence: Fajardo attributes damage to removal of people from cultivation. Pineda’s separate report concerns skills, yards and wages. Both are colonial administrators’ accounts.
rubric.chronology_geography: The 1595 wreck, later Mexican jar and 1726 register stay separate. Schematic port links do not reconstruct individual voyages.
rubric.perspective: The Coast Miwok archaeological context supports locally situated questions. Proposed uses of fragments retain their status as interpretations.
rubric.reading: The account explains the gap between a named consignment and a complete cargo total.
rubric.activity: The later earthenware jar and wreck porcelain give a child a concrete reason to separate observation from cargo identification.
rubric.connections: The Pacific context supports comparison of trading systems. Each object still needs its own acquisition and movement evidence.

dossier_audits.reviewer: Codex author review and targeted source checks

dossier_audits.name: Ming workshops and court design

existing_interval.label: 1368–1644 CE
existing_interval.note: Conventional Ming dynastic period. Individual works and trade routes retain their own dates.

rubric.orientation: The fish jar supplies a concrete object for asking who designed, made, selected and bought porcelain.
rubric.explanation: The text describes decoration below and above glaze, then follows decisions from court designs to finished wares and disposal.
rubric.evidence: The Palace Museum distinguishes destruction of rejected ware from collection and burial of ware damaged in use.
rubric.chronology_geography: The Jiajing-period example and 1542 order for similar jars remain separate from the conventional Ming interval and the 1608 institutional change.

rubric.explanation: The House of Books brings translation, calligraphy, binding and painting together.

rubric.reading: Marginal attributions in a different manuscript give the adult reader a bounded way to explore specialization.

dossier_audits.name: Banda: monopoly and forced displacement

existing_interval.label: 1621 CE
existing_interval.note: The dated conquest investigated here; Bandanese history extends before and after this event.

dossier_audits.name: Uruk and the work of recordkeeping

existing_interval.label: c. 3100–2900 BCE
existing_interval.note: Date of the selected administrative tablet, not the beginning or end of Uruk.

rubric.orientation: The tablet provides a concrete entry to grain accounting in southern Mesopotamia. The city locator and the probable provenance stay distinguishable.

rubric.connections: Dholavira and Liangzhu let the reader compare coordination of work without assuming an exchange route or a shared government.

dossier_audits.name: Old Kingdom Egypt: lives in a tomb wall

existing_interval.label: c. 2649–2130 BCE
existing_interval.note: Approximate period convention in the current 2019 essay, whose URL retains an older endpoint.

rubric.orientation: The Saqqara chapel introduces a question about commemoration. The text moves explicitly to different evidence from Giza.

rubric.connections: The Uruk comparison gives two records of provision with different purposes, while the Caral comparison broadens the question to sustaining construction.

dossier_audits.name: Dholavira: a city built around water

existing_interval.label: c. 3000–1500 BCE
existing_interval.note: Occupation range in the UNESCO site account; mature urban phases and individual objects have narrower dates.

rubric.orientation: The city on Khadir Island supplies the water-management problem. The regional Indus seal has its own provenance.

rubric.activity: The solid structures and dashed survey area let a learner make one observation and one excavation prediction from supplied material.
rubric.connections: The Liangzhu comparison works through dated built features and what evidence of coordination can tell us about households.

dossier_audits.name: Liangzhu: waterworks, rice and jade

existing_interval.label: c. 3300–2300 BCE
existing_interval.note: UNESCO’s city/site range. The Met’s broader Liangzhu culture label c3200–2000 BCE has a different scope.

rubric.orientation: The Lower Yangtze city, regional dams and an individual jade are introduced as three scales of inquiry.
rubric.explanation: Grass-wrapped clay makes dam construction intelligible as a chain of material tasks. The text separates reconstructed capacity from use and allocation.

rubric.reading: The material and opening can be observed before readers consider the paper’s correction and calibrated years BP.
rubric.activity: The guide supports sorting a material, structure and activity. The final question explicitly asks for a social question the artifacts leave open.
rubric.connections: Dholavira offers a comparison of water management and uncertain household access, preserving separate local systems.

dossier_audits.name: Caral-Supe: building a shared place

existing_interval.label: c. 3000–1800 BCE
existing_interval.note: UNESCO’s radiocarbon-based development range is followed. A current Peruvian government orientation gives 3000–1900 BCE; different endpoints are retained.

alternatives.label: 3000–1900 BCE in the Peruvian government orientation

rubric.orientation: The Supe Valley site is placed inland from the coast. The opening ties public architecture to recurrent provision and renewal.

rubric.reading: The diagram supplies a simple spatial sequence first. The deeper text explains sampling, dates and the problems with turning microscopic counts into portions.

rubric.connections: The Old Kingdom and Skara comparisons ask how buildings were renewed and supplied in distinct places.

dossier_audits.name: Skara Brae: households in stone

existing_interval.label: c. 3180–2500 BCE
existing_interval.note: Structured date in HES’s selected tool record gives the contextual range. Its narrative instead says 3100–2400; house-history page places the end around 2500. Boundaries are approximate.

rubric.orientation: The stone interiors at Sandwick introduce domestic work. The locator identifies the present site without projecting its coastline backward.
rubric.explanation: Buildings, hearths and passages explain how heating, storage and access depended on maintenance and changes to adjoining structures.

rubric.activity: The learner traces an imagined route and identifies evidence needed to test it. A measured ancient floor plan is unnecessary for that exercise.
rubric.connections: Caral offers a comparison of household renewal. The wider Orkney monuments have separate functions and dates.

dossier_audits.name: Hattusha and the problem of collapse

existing_interval.label: 13th century BCE, approaching c. 1200
existing_interval.note: Investigation window for the late capital and political transformation; not the city’s entire occupation or an exact destruction year.

rubric.orientation: The opening distinguishes life in a capital and the loss of its central administration. It locates Hattusha and the separate Gordion tree samples.
rubric.explanation: The grain-store example shows how consecutive short harvests could reduce reserves. The text leaves access, choices and withdrawal as further causal questions.

rubric.reading: The mechanism of recurring shortages comes before the technical discussion of detrending and isotope evidence.

rubric.connections: Uluburun supplies a contemporary regional comparison of institutions and provisioning without turning drought into a cause of the shipwreck.

dossier_audits.name: Uluburun: a cargo beneath the sea

existing_interval.label: c. 1320 BCE ±15 years
existing_interval.note: Dating reported by the excavators’ project page; not an exact sailing or sinking year.

rubric.orientation: The Kaş wreck location anchors the cargo question. The displayed point can be found without inferring a complete voyage.
rubric.explanation: The account moves from recovered materials to the shipbuilding, packing and maintenance that allowed them to travel together.

rubric.reading: A learner can sort two cargo items and one unknown. An adult can follow differing ore-source arguments and the separate scope of later wreck studies.
rubric.activity: The evidence guide distinguishes recovered cargo, inferred metal provenance and an unknown itinerary. Each category has an example in the capsule.
rubric.connections: The Hattusha and Shang comparisons use institutions and craft as questions. The mixed freight does not establish contact with either selected object.

dossier_audits.name: Shang: ritual, writing and bronze

existing_interval.label: c. 1600–1046 BCE
existing_interval.note: Conventional Shang period in the current museum sources; individual objects can have narrower dates.

rubric.orientation: The setting distinguishes late Anyang from the longer Shang chronology and from the two objects’ place attributions.
rubric.explanation: Making a hollow bronze and recording a divination charge are described as different skilled sequences. The lesson’s translated examples refer to their own objects.

rubric.reading: The family can compare the two surfaces before considering workshop organization and unequal power in the adult reading.

rubric.connections: Dong Son and Uluburun offer bounded comparisons of bronze and production. The prompt avoids attributing any one museum object to Fu Hao’s tomb.

dossier_audits.name: Kerma, Egypt and a traveling beaker

existing_interval.label: c. 2050–1500 BCE
existing_interval.note: Middle and Classical Kerma frame in the regional chronology; not the full history of Nubia.

rubric.orientation: The visually distinctive beaker is the entry into a Nubian capital. Giving Abydos tomb 525 separately prevents the regional marker being mistaken for the findspot.
rubric.explanation: Hand-forming, finishing and firing connect practical steps to the vessel. Courtyards and provisioning widen the inquiry from craft to the city.

rubric.reading: The family can begin by drawing the color boundary. The deeper account explains how excavation overturned the earlier trading-post interpretation.
rubric.activity: Surface, documented grave and imagined biography are separable using the photograph and capsule alone. The activity requires no real firing.
rubric.connections: The Taharqo comparison asks about making and institutions at different dates. The Olmec link compares techniques and the interpretation of craft evidence.

dossier_audits.name: Olmec communities and material worlds

existing_interval.label: c. 1200–400 BCE
existing_interval.note: Cultural and artistic flourishing frame in Doyle’s essay; not one kingdom’s precise lifespan.

rubric.orientation: The small ceramic figure provides a way into the distinct histories of San Lorenzo and La Venta. Its own findspot is unspecified.
rubric.explanation: Ear ornaments open a question about bodily display, while floor samples, redistributed soil and workshop traces supply distinct scales of production.
rubric.evidence: The Met record measures the ceramic figure at 17 cm and discusses possible social meanings. Its scale supports comparison with a monument while its ornaments alone cannot identify an office.

rubric.reading: Readers can begin with the ornaments and hands. The deeper account gives each inference between an auger sample, a building and an estimated population.
rubric.activity: Two visible features and one further question can be supplied from the figure and caption. Alternative interpretations of adornment remain possible.
rubric.connections: Poverty Point and Kerma permit comparison of materials and organized work. Each retains a distinct chronology and evidence for settlement.

dossier_audits.name: Lapita: pottery and island voyaging

existing_interval.label: c. 1500–500 BCE
existing_interval.note: Broad pottery-style frame in the museum essay; regional settlement and later histories have different dates.

rubric.orientation: The introduction sets the Bismarck Archipelago alongside several later island communities rather than assigning a single journey to every Lapita find.
rubric.explanation: The account connects making a pot, transporting materials and feeding an island settlement. The Rove case distinguishes nonlocal temper from an inferred transfer of finished pottery.
rubric.evidence: The Teouma authors analyzed bone-collagen isotopes from 49 adults against a dietary baseline. The dossier keeps the protein measure and its local group distinct from every meal on every island.
rubric.chronology_geography: The coral files at Nukuleka, their deposition and subsequent plain-pottery histories have independent dates. The later c. 400 BCE estimate marks ceramic change.
rubric.perspective: Islanders appear as navigators, potters and food producers. The linguistic reconstruction has separate evidence, and decoration cannot identify an individual speaker.
rubric.reading: The learner can repeat a drawn pattern before the deeper discussion of dating models, redeposition and linguistic arguments.
rubric.activity: The activity explicitly uses a learner-made motif and asks what material or dated evidence would be needed to infer movement. The response criteria allow drawing or explanation.
rubric.connections: Polynesian voyaging offers a later inquiry into maritime skills. Kuk adds another independently dated setting for production.

dossier_audits.name: Nimrud: power on palace walls

existing_interval.label: Reign of Ashurnasirpal II, 883–859 BCE
existing_interval.note: Selected palace-building and representational context; not the full duration of Assyria or Nimrud.

rubric.orientation: The protective figure and the writing on the palace wall open a question about the royal audience at Kalhu.
rubric.explanation: Quarrying, moving and carving stone and arranging the reliefs connect skilled labor to an official account of kingship. The later administrative command seeks a practical result.
rubric.evidence: Seymour identifies local gypsum slabs on a mud-brick palace and describes the challenges of transport and carving. The gallery combines reliefs from several rooms.
rubric.chronology_geography: The palace belongs to the reign of 883–859 BCE. The composite plan includes later features and the letter’s editorial date is about 732 BCE.
rubric.perspective: People moved by force appear in a royal claim and in an order to officials. Neither voice represents their own testimony or demonstrates fulfillment.
rubric.reading: The relief’s wings and bucket provide a family entry. The adult track asks how a plan or a coercive command can be read against the purpose of its maker.
rubric.activity: Children describe a visible feature and then use the capsule to explain the inferred protective setting. No translation from a photograph is required.
rubric.connections: Ashoka and Taharqo allow comparison of royal communication and display. Different texts, buildings and audiences give each comparison a specific limit.

dossier_audits.name: Ashoka: messages carved in stone

existing_interval.label: Ashoka, c. 268–232 BCE
existing_interval.note: Reign convention used by Neelis. Other chronologies place accession earlier; not exact dates for every edict.

rubric.orientation: Selected inscription sites give the question about communicating across languages distinct places and audiences.
rubric.explanation: Edicts connect practical tasks such as wells and planting with instructions to judicial officers. Describing the actions makes their implementation open to investigation.
rubric.evidence: Neelis distinguishes the broader moral and administrative policies from Buddhist doctrine and explicitly identifies donations to the Ajivikas alongside Buddhist patronage.
rubric.chronology_geography: The Sarnath marker orients one pillar. Girnar, Dhauli and Kandahar have different texts and versions. The 1925 English edition precedes the later discoveries.
rubric.perspective: Officials and subjects have different roles in these texts. The king’s remorse and promise of care sit alongside the coercion of conquest and the absence of measured outcomes.
rubric.reading: The family track turns a named task into a question about work. The deeper track explains edition, language, distribution and the regional edict substitutions.
rubric.activity: The three-site matching task can be done from the supplied map and capsules. The answer asks for independent evidence that would test an announcement.
rubric.connections: Qin standardization and Athenian institutions provide points of comparison for instructions and their reception. Readers have to identify the evidence for each.

dossier_audits.name: Athens: who worked in public?

existing_interval.label: Sixth–fourth centuries BCE
existing_interval.note: Analytical window joining an Archaic vase to Classical evidence. These phases are distinguished in the text; not a single unchanging social system.

rubric.orientation: The hydria starts a question about working in a public space and participating in civic decisions in Athens.
rubric.explanation: The water task and the scrutiny for civic enrollment expose two different conditions for participation. Wealth and enslavement affected the distribution of work.

dossier_audits.name: Taharqo: a Kushite king’s afterlife

existing_interval.label: Taharqo’s reign, c. 690–664 BCE
existing_interval.note: Catalogue reign dates; the figure is attributed to this period, not one exact production year.

rubric.orientation: The granite shabti supplies a starting question about power, work and elite expectations in Kushite Egypt and Sudan.

dossier_audits.name: A Chavín textile: traveling images?

existing_interval.label: Fourth–third centuries BCE
existing_interval.note: Current object catalogue dating, reflecting research cited in 2023; not the lifespan of a Chavín state.

rubric.orientation: Painted shapes on a woven cloth introduce how an image might travel while the object’s own route stays uncertain.

existing_interval.note: Conventional dynasty dates; individual objects and political disruptions have their own chronology.

dossier_audits.name: Abbasid Iraq: cities, surfaces and changing power

existing_interval.label: Abbasid rule in Baghdad: conventional frame, 750–1258 CE
existing_interval.note: Baghdad founded 762; court at Samarra 836–892. Authority changed substantially; later nominal caliphs in Egypt are outside this frame.

rubric.orientation: A lustre-painted bowl invites the reader to follow techniques across changing courts.

journey_audits.title: What makes a community visible?
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose two kinds of evidence. What can each show, and what does each leave difficult to know?
journey_audits.audience_fit: chapter route, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Begin by estimating what a single sign or image communicates. The detour from Liangzhu to Caral explicitly invites comparison across oceans, and the backward jump to Skara Brae ends at household scale.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: Grain signs, burials and buildings give a learner different questions to pose. Compare the tablet’s probable reading with what the Indus seal leaves unresolved.

journey_audits.title: Connected worlds, different disruptions
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Explain one connection we can demonstrate, one proposed cause we must qualify, and one distant history that should not be folded into the same story.
journey_audits.audience_fit: chapter route, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: The wreck and drought open a causal question in the eastern Mediterranean. The move back to Kerma and sideways to China, Mexico and the Pacific tests where that question stops traveling.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: At Gordion the measured record is tree growth and isotope variation. A causal story about choices at Hattusha needs independent political evidence.

journey_audits.title: Power, work and whose voice survives
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose a record and name a person whose experience it might leave out.
journey_audits.audience_fit: chapter route, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Royal messages in Nimrud and South Asia precede domestic water work, funerary evidence, a portable textile, administrative records and bronze casting. Geography and the source change together.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The court’s announcement is evidence of the sender’s claim. Testing effects on ruled people gives the return question an answerable direction.

journey_audits.title: The world around 200 CE
journey_audits.existing_duration: 25–40 minutes, or one stop at a time
journey_audits.learning_outcome: What changed in your picture of the world around 200 CE? Name one supported connection and one comparison that does not imply contact.
journey_audits.audience_fit: chapter route, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Each stop holds the atlas year at 200 CE while changing region. The earlier Kanishka coin and later Aksum monuments teach the distinction between the comparison year and an object date.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The Han tower and Colima model invite comparison of visible forms and possible uses. The Mexican and Chinese cases supply no direct connection between the two objects.

journey_audits.title: Institutions, images and the work of continuity
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose a long historical label and explain one important change inside it.
journey_audits.audience_fit: chapter route, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Move between capitals, a vessel, a building and a teaching center. Reversals from 950 to 750 make this a comparison of institutions across time.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: Nalanda contains earlier archaeology and later evidence for a scholastic establishment. Different dates make the final request for change inside a long label possible.

journey_audits.title: Cities, craft and knowledge in motion
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Explain one demonstrated connection and one connection that remains a question.
journey_audits.audience_fit: chapter route, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Move from Mali to the Middle Niger, Angkor and Song, then to Andean cloth and Pacific wayfinding. The geographic jumps require a fresh claim about connection at each stop.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The tunic’s construction can support comparison. An individual itinerary requires a different source. The return asks which relationship the learner can actually demonstrate.

journey_audits.title: Ocean connections, 1450–1650
journey_audits.existing_duration: 30–45 minutes, or one encounter at a time
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose two ocean connections. How did their mechanisms, power relationships and surviving evidence differ?
journey_audits.audience_fit: chapter route, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Port negotiations lead into patronage and religious interpretation, then books, kilns and two colonial trading systems. The sequence groups encounters by mechanism even as some object dates overlap.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: Coen’s account describes company action in Banda from a company official’s perspective. Use other voices to test effects on Bandanese people.

journey_audits.title: Machines, work and who can choose
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Name one change in production and one separate question about power over work.
journey_audits.audience_fit: chapter route, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Proceed from Haitian independence through the factory investigation and Tomioka to Hine’s photograph. At each stop distinguish changes in production from power over the worker.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The image depicts a setting. The caption attributes the overseer’s reported words to Hine’s account. A claim about lasting protection needs follow-up evidence.

journey_audits.title: Political freedom and the meaning of a promise
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose a promise and explain whose experience would help test it.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Move forward from te Tiriti to Partition and the South African constitution. They are different kinds of political instruments whose effects require distinct local evidence.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: Read the selected right as a commitment. A learner can name people affected and specify the record or experience that would help test implementation.

journey_audits.title: Global war, state power and a new signal
journey_audits.learning_outcome: What does a public image encourage you to see, and what evidence would broaden that view?
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Move from a wartime recruiting poster through the regional chronologies of the Second World War to reporting about Sputnik. The three sources serve different purposes.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The supported answer distinguishes war in Asia, war in Europe and the Holocaust’s chronology. The family exercise uses the dates already supplied.

journey_audits.title: Earth, food and gathering in Indigenous North America
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose one object or landscape. State an observation, a supported explanation and one thing it cannot tell you.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: The sequence moves through four distinct landscapes in chronological order, from Poverty Point to Cahokia. Changing scale from an object to an entire community requires independent evidence.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The cacao result applies to a small set of fragments from Pueblo Bonito. Compare the architecture photograph with the chemical report before making an argument about consumption.

journey_audits.title: Books, silk and power: West/Central Asia, 1500–1800
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose one luxury object and explain a chain of work around it. Identify one person or experience the object alone cannot recover.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Compare distinct centers for copying and painting, İznik ceramics, New Julfa’s trading community and a later lacquer case. The proposed movement of one manuscript differs from forced population movement.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The silk evidence permits a discussion of work and trade. The 1604 deportation prevents later commercial prominence from being read back as consent.

journey_audits.title: Arctic, coast and Plains: work, knowledge and belonging
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose one northern object or landscape. Keep one observation, one supported explanation and one question that requires another kind of evidence.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Move across distinct communities and much later sources, from Bering Sea carving to a twentieth-century institutional milestone. The Ozette stop explicitly warns that its burial date is disputed.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: Hidatsa gardening and Makah cedar work allow a comparison of practical needs. Community accounts and selected material remains support different parts of that comparison.

journey_audits.title: Eastern Woodlands: communities, knowledge and power
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Keep an observation, a supported explanation and a question. Revisit this place or record with another type of source.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: The jump backward from Ocmulgee to Ohio is deliberate. The later sequence moves from a Wendat village into treaty, newspaper and harvesting records from different communities.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: A written promise or editorial claim can be read closely. The family can identify a second source needed to show implementation and lived effects.

journey_audits.title: Independence, citizenship and the work after a promise
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose two cases. Name the power that changed, the evidence for that change and one outcome that needs more investigation.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Four later-twentieth-century milestones run forward. The stops distinguish Indonesian proclamation and recognition, Partition’s boundary announcement, transfer of power in Ghana and South African constitutional commitments.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: A declaration, altered stamp and voting photograph establish different kinds of event. The return makes the learner identify the power that actually changed.

journey_audits.title: Who did the work? Accounts, reservoirs and rice
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose two cases. For each, name the practical task, the evidence for organization and one household-level question the source cannot answer.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Move from accounting to water systems in Dholavira and Liangzhu; the last stop moves back in time. Coordination is the shared question, with independent evidence at each place.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The family can point to selected items in a grain record. Waterworks support a different argument from one household’s daily obligations.

journey_audits.title: Institutions, shipments and ritual
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose two cases. Name what is observed or recovered, what is inferred about organization, and one new source that could test the inference.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Begin with excavated cargo, then test a proxy-climate inference and finally inspect a bronze. Neither contemporaneity nor one record type obliges all the objects to share an institutional history.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: Cargo shows association, trees measure environmental conditions and casting leaves physical traces. A worker’s name or a ship’s entire itinerary needs separate proof.

journey_audits.title: Rules, messages and public work
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose two cases. Explain who had to do something for a rule to work, and name one source that could test what happened.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: The stops move backward from Qin administration through Ashoka’s public messages to an Athenian water scene. The comparison concerns rules and the work needed to put them into practice.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: A pictured task does not settle political eligibility. Dated local administrative records can test how a formal standard was applied.

journey_audits.title: Objects, work and exchange
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose two records. Explain the work or relationship each makes visible, then name evidence needed before drawing a route between their places.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Begin at a Palmyrene family memorial, move back to a dated inscription and coin context, then ahead to Aksum. The move between commercial places raises a question about relationships.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The Palmyrene inscription identifies family members. Establishing a caravan investment requires a record connecting those particular people to that particular venture.

journey_audits.title: Spaces, skills and learning
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose one institution. Explain a practical task and who helped perform it, then name evidence needed before claiming everyone had the same access.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: The gate diagram frames access at Chang’an; the Abbasid bowl changes the question to making, and Nalanda to sustaining study. These overlapping periods do not describe one institution’s development.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: A dated gate rule and evidence about actual entry test the imagined errand. The family can distinguish its modern diagram from observations of a resident’s trip.

journey_audits.title: Work, obligation and historical voices
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose one case. Explain a practical task, name the voice describing it, and identify evidence needed before saying the arrangement benefited its workers.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Move forward from the Song memorial to the ruler on the Catalan Atlas and the Andean tunic. At each transition identify whose priorities the evidence reveals.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: Specify a household, local borrowing and repayment evidence before judging its experience of the proposed loan. The family can trace the proposal from reserves to tax collection.

journey_audits.title: Makers, interpreters and unequal encounters
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose a task, identify the source that reveals it, and explain what further evidence would help establish the worker’s choices.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Pass from Malindi and Calicut to Benin and Kongo. The voyage provides a pilot and interpreter; African workshops and royal correspondence supply different roles and voices.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The journal and its diagram show why pilotage and interpretation mattered. They leave workers’ choices for a separate inquiry.

journey_audits.title: Homes, provisions and renewal
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose one task. Explain who or what had to contribute, cite the record that supports it, and name one question needing further evidence.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Compare provision at Giza, rebuilding at Caral and practical work inside a Scottish dwelling. The last stop moves to an earlier context to return to household work.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: A phased house or reused room can reveal repeated work. The final answer must identify a specific task and the record that supports it.

journey_audits.title: Clay, work and local histories
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose one practical task and one proposed connection. Name the evidence that supports each, then choose a further test that would answer the remaining question.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Poverty Point heating objects, a small Olmec figure and Lapita stamping connect through work with clay. The chronological movement gives no archaeological chain of transmission between these regions.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: Mineral comparison against possible source clays and secure dating would test a proposed transfer. The pattern task illustrates a manufacturing operation.

journey_audits.title: Makers, supplies and royal claims
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose one making task and one claim about its organisation. Name the supporting evidence, whose voice it preserves and a further source that could improve the explanation.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Move through Kerma pottery, rooms and provision at Nimrud, and Taharqo’s royal representation. Technical and administrative evidence address different parts of organized work.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The order provides evidence for a request. A delivery or recipient record would test whether people carried it out.

journey_audits.title: Images, spaces and work
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose one activity, show the evidence that supports it, and name one additional source that could explain who organized or performed the work.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Start with Chavín textile imagery, then compare a Teotihuacan household context and a Moche vessel. The last two share a timeline anchor while the source type changes.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: A vessel’s surface supports observation. Secure archaeological context and technical comparison would strengthen an attribution to an individual workshop.

journey_audits.title: Objects, places and associations
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Choose one claim, identify its supporting object or place record, and ask for one additional source that could test it.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: A Đông Sơn object, Colima model and surveyed Ohio earthwork raise three questions about associating an artifact or later view with a specific place.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The model’s roof is observable and its possible use as an incense-burner lid is a catalogue interpretation. The learner can name which part needs new evidence.

journey_audits.title: Places, patrons and work
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Name one kind of work, identify its supporting evidence, and ask which person or institution remains to be explained.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Proceed from a Maya inscription to Borobudur’s reconstructed forms to carved ivory and a separately excavated harbor. The cases offer different evidence for people who supported work.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The published schematic allows comparison of square and circular forms. Establishing a compulsory ancient walking route needs dated evidence of use.

journey_audits.title: Buildings, food and continuing connections
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Name one kind of work, identify its supporting record and ask whose experience or which date remains to be explained.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Compare Pueblo Bonito’s historic plan, Cahokia’s later view and Ocmulgee’s earthlodge feature plan. Each stop distinguishes the age of the record from the urban activity it helps explain.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: Room groupings can be checked on the plan; interpretation of habitation needs excavation. The drawing supplies no roster of ancient residents.

journey_audits.title: Makers, patrons and markets
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Name one task, identify its supporting source and ask which worker, audience or working relationship remains to be explained.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Move between a Ming fish jar, Ottoman court and ceramic work, and Mughal bookmaking. Similar centuries leave changes of patron, workshop and buyer to be established separately.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The image supports an observation about arrangement. Materials, a related court order and wider production belong to catalogues and documentary sources.

journey_audits.title: Households, books and city work
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Name a supporting task, its source and one person or household whose experience remains unknown.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Begin with a Bukhara manuscript, then move to Isfahan’s forced relocation and commercial work and a Zand object. This sequence distinguishes a depicted reception from household and urban work.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: The catalogue qualifies copying and painting as separate stages. The photograph alone cannot identify every worker or assign all parts to one city.

journey_audits.title: Goods, work and coercion
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Name one task, its source and a person’s experience or movement that still needs evidence.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Two stops connect VOC coercion in Banda with the differently dated and governed Manila trade. The Mexican jar and the registered 1726 consignment are deliberately separated.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: A record of shipped goods can support a claim at shipment scale. Assigning the particular jar to a vessel or a Banda–Manila route needs direct evidence.

journey_audits.title: Skills, records and protection
journey_audits.learning_outcome: Name a practical task, the source explaining it and one separate question about working conditions that still needs evidence.
journey_audits.audience_fit: additional investigation, family with adult and self-directed tracks
journey_audits.sequence_review: Use an 1836 factory investigation, a depiction of silk reeling and a later Hine photograph to distinguish enforcement, technical education and advocacy.
journey_audits.evidence_task_review: A drawing can help identify a skill, and a report records an inquiry. Establishing effective protection requires evidence from workers or subsequent enforcement.

comparison_audits.current_question: How can learning a production skill differ from putting worker protection into practice?
comparison_audits.source_review: Both cases show that industrial change needed skilled people. Teaching reeling at Tomioka can document how a technique spread. An inspector’s report can document how a British complaint was investigated. They answer different questions about working conditions.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: Both cases show that industrial change needed skilled people. Teaching reeling at Tomioka can document how a technique spread. An inspector’s report can document how a British complaint was investigated. They answer different questions about working conditions.

comparison_audits.current_question: Whose work is visible in these commercial and colonial records, and whose experience needs other evidence?
comparison_audits.source_review: Shipbuilding and repairs in the Manila system and cultivating and processing spices on Banda reveal the work behind trade. A colonial report on an imposed monopoly cannot speak for the Bandanese, and wreck cargo cannot measure consent among Philippine workers.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: Shipbuilding and repairs in the Manila system and cultivating and processing spices on Banda reveal the work behind trade. A colonial report on an imposed monopoly cannot speak for the Bandanese, and wreck cargo cannot measure consent among Philippine workers.

comparison_audits.current_question: Which records explain the work supporting city life, and whose experience remains unknown?
comparison_audits.source_review: A merchant family’s letter makes separation visible at New Julfa, while manuscript and endowment records identify bookmaking and maintenance in Bukhara. Each reflects people with access to particular institutions. Neither represents every urban household.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: A merchant family’s letter makes separation visible at New Julfa, while manuscript and endowment records identify bookmaking and maintenance in Bukhara. Each reflects people with access to particular institutions. Neither represents every urban household.

comparison_audits.current_question: How can an object’s attribution be kept separate from a city’s households and political history?
comparison_audits.source_review: The carpet’s possible production centres and the lacquer case’s attributed painter offer different degrees of identification. Accounts of Safavid Isfahan and later Zand Shiraz provide context without revealing either object’s particular purchaser or workshop.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: The carpet’s possible production centres and the lacquer case’s attributed painter offer different degrees of identification. Accounts of Safavid Isfahan and later Zand Shiraz provide context without revealing either object’s particular purchaser or workshop.

comparison_audits.current_question: What distinguishes evidence of court demand from evidence of making and buying?
comparison_audits.source_review: The Ming vessel’s reign mark and an Ottoman decorator’s name identify different relationships to production. Court designs, commissions, workshop debris and market records provide separate checks on whether an item was ordered, made or bought.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: The Ming vessel’s reign mark and an Ottoman decorator’s name identify different relationships to production. Court designs, commissions, workshop debris and market records provide separate checks on whether an item was ordered, made or bought.

comparison_audits.current_question: How do writing and decoration connect specialized work with patrons and audiences?
comparison_audits.source_review: A Mughal manuscript project organized translators, writers and painters. An Ottoman object can preserve a decorator’s name, while production debris records other tasks. Individuals named in either setting provide only part of a workshop’s history.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: A Mughal manuscript project organized translators, writers and painters. An Ottoman object can preserve a decorator’s name, while production debris records other tasks. Individuals named in either setting provide only part of a workshop’s history.

comparison_audits.current_question: How can building records and particular samples explain work without dating a whole people?
comparison_audits.source_review: Masonry and food remains at Chaco and modeled clay at Ocmulgee show people building and using places. Dates belong to particular structures or samples. A later council account adds living significance without identifying every ancient institution.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: Masonry and food remains at Chaco and modeled clay at Ocmulgee show people building and using places. Dates belong to particular structures or samples. A later council account adds living significance without identifying every ancient institution.

comparison_audits.current_question: How do local evidence and attributed community accounts change explanations of settlement?
comparison_audits.source_review: Cahokia’s changing neighborhoods and unfinished copper show work at particular locations. At Ocmulgee a revised building chronology and community accounts add other kinds of evidence. Neither settlement stands for the history of every descendant community.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: Cahokia’s changing neighborhoods and unfinished copper show work at particular locations. At Ocmulgee a revised building chronology and community accounts add other kinds of evidence. Neither settlement stands for the history of every descendant community.

comparison_audits.current_question: How can evidence for making, supporting and maintaining a place reveal different institutions?
comparison_audits.source_review: Harbour timbers record practical repair at Constantinople, while Borobudur’s galleries and drainage reveal construction and later maintenance. The devotional ivory and modern conservation add context at different dates. Neither establishes the full workforce behind a monument.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: Harbour timbers record practical repair at Constantinople, while Borobudur’s galleries and drainage reveal construction and later maintenance. The devotional ivory and modern conservation add context at different dates. Neither establishes the full workforce behind a monument.

comparison_audits.current_question: How do a portable image, an owner’s name and separate work contexts support different explanations?
comparison_audits.source_review: Both portable objects invite questions about purpose and access. A Maya cup can name its owner. The ivory’s devotional use depends on interpretation. Separate household and harbour excavations cannot identify the workshop for either object.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: Both portable objects invite questions about purpose and access. A Maya cup can name its owner. The ivory’s devotional use depends on interpretation. Separate household and harbour excavations cannot identify the workshop for either object.

comparison_audits.current_question: How do documented deposits and later place records change an explanation of shared material forms?
comparison_audits.source_review: In Vietnam a group of tools inside a drum documents one deposit. In Ohio a trench and an early plan document particular earthwork features. Later moulds or a modern community account add dated perspectives without establishing one purpose or linked route.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: In Vietnam a group of tools inside a drum documents one deposit. In Ohio a trench and an early plan document particular earthwork features. Later moulds or a modern community account add dated perspectives without establishing one purpose or linked route.

comparison_audits.current_question: What can visible form, an excavated association and a later reconstruction each establish about a place?
comparison_audits.source_review: A Colima model preserves roof and stair forms. A separately excavated tomb supplies an association; Ohio earthwork plans and trenches record built features. A reconstruction at either scale needs evidence beyond resemblance and cannot supply the model’s exact findspot.

Isfahan’s silk economy also included rural producers and merchants affected by coerced Armenian relocation. A surviving dish or carpet cannot measure the benefits to those workers.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: Ottoman court specialists and ceramic makers worked for multiple patrons and markets. Isfahan’s silk economy also included rural producers and merchants affected by coerced Armenian relocation. A surviving dish or carpet cannot measure the benefits to those workers.

comparison_audits.current_question: How do changing patrons affect books and decorative arts?
comparison_audits.source_review: An illustrated book from Bukhara preserves a patronage context and separates copying from painting. A Zand lacquer case has an attributed maker, but its purchaser is unknown. Differences between those records limit what can be inferred about changes in buyers’ tastes.

A Zand lacquer case has an attributed maker, but its purchaser is unknown. Differences between those records limit what can be inferred about changes in buyers’ tastes.

comparison_audits.current_question: How do tools and clothing carry skilled knowledge?
comparison_audits.source_review: A carved Bering Sea ivory component shows fitting and engraving but cannot recover a whole hunt. For Inuinnait sewing, a historical photograph and a later community-led reconstruction illuminate different stages of inquiry. The two cases are separated by many centuries.

For Inuinnait sewing, a historical photograph and a later community-led reconstruction illuminate different stages of inquiry. The two cases are separated by many centuries.

comparison_audits.current_question: How do surviving belongings relate to community knowledge and authority?
comparison_audits.source_review: Makah oral history and excavation give the recovered Ozette household materials a community setting. Kwakwaka’wakw histories of confiscation and return explain separate responsibilities surrounding potlatch belongings. Evidence that an object survived cannot establish who had authority over its use.

comparison_audits.current_question: How do communities coordinate food, work and seasonal knowledge?
comparison_audits.source_review: Blackfoot accounts connect coordinated bison hunting with obligations extending beyond the kill. Hidatsa gardens, storage and women’s roles in earthlodge construction show work over a village year. Each account places hunting and seasonal knowledge within a particular community.

comparison_audits.current_question: What can a public building and a village reveal about collective life?
comparison_audits.source_review: Ocmulgee’s clay remains and revised construction dates concern a particular earthlodge. At the Wendat site of Laine, a modeled date range estimates village occupation. Neither a revised sample nor a probability plot supplies a precise founding date for a people.

comparison_audits.current_question: How do words and records carry political responsibilities?
comparison_audits.source_review: Canandaigua treaty clauses document commitments whose fulfillment must be investigated. Cherokee-language print enabled national debate during the approach to removal. A treaty image and a newspaper each preserve political words without recording universal agreement or implementation.

comparison_audits.current_question: How do material work and knowledge connect across generations?
comparison_audits.source_review: Ojibwe accounts place ricing and the finishing of manoomin within relationships of responsibility. Inuinnait sewing combines learned techniques with changing materials. Photographs and later reconstructions have separate dates and can reveal different parts of that knowledge.

asymmetry_review.historicalJudgment: Ojibwe accounts place ricing and the finishing of manoomin within relationships of responsibility. comparison_audits.current_question: How do royal images, work claims and excavated production answer different questions about authority?
comparison_audits.source_review: The Nimrud palace required quarrying, carving and continuing service. Taharqo’s Kawa texts claim royal organization, while workshop debris at Sanam records faience making. Royal language and the excavation of a workshop give different access to workers’ status and choices.

comparison_audits.current_question: What can different materials and find contexts tell us about skilled work and institutions?
comparison_audits.source_review: Kerma’s pottery and excavated craft areas relate differently to production than a royal shabti does. A faience fragment matches the Sanam mould, while the selected granite figure is only probably associated with Nuri. Geographic proximity cannot supply its workshop or a continuous labor system.
